core_themes.name: Opaque and inconsistent fee practices
core_themes.claim: Letting agents charge tenants fees in widely varying amounts and formats, often not clearly displayed or itemised, making it hard for tenants to understand or compare costs.

core_themes.name: Tenants' lack of bargaining power
core_themes.claim: Because landlords, not tenants, appoint and pay the letting agent, tenants have little or no ability to negotiate, avoid or opt out of the fees charged to them.

core_themes.name: Misaligned incentives and weak competition on tenant fees
core_themes.claim: Landlords and agents are incentivised to compete on landlord-side fees but have no incentive to minimise or compete on tenant-side fees, which can even be used to subsidise lower landlord fees or result in double-charging.

core_themes.name: Scale, growth and financial harm of fees
core_themes.claim: Tenant letting fees are widespread, have risen significantly in recent years, and impose real financial hardship, deterring moves and making it harder to save for a deposit.

core_themes.name: Rationale for shifting fees to landlords
core_themes.claim: Because landlords hold the stronger market position and choose the agent, banning tenant fees and making landlords bear agent costs will sharpen competition among agents and improve transparency.

core_themes.name: Insufficiency of existing transparency regulation
core_themes.claim: Earlier transparency requirements under the Consumer Rights Act 2015 have not proven effective at improving standards or enabling tenants to shop around, justifying a stronger intervention such as a ban.

core_themes.name: Scottish precedent as supporting evidence
core_themes.claim: Evidence from Scotland's long-standing ban on tenant letting fees shows that such a ban can operate with minimal negative side-effects on landlords, agents or the rental sector, supporting the case for a similar ban in England.

core_themes.name: Scope of the ban
core_themes.claim: The ban should cover all fees, premiums or charges linked to granting, renewing or continuing a tenancy, whether charged by agents, landlords or third parties, so that tenants pay only rent and a refundable deposit.

core_themes.name: Anticipated costs and benefits
core_themes.claim: While some agent costs may be passed through into higher rents, competitive pressure will limit full pass-through, and the ban will yield benefits including lower upfront costs, easier moving, reduced homelessness risk and easier saving for a deposit.

core_themes.name: Primary enforcement by local authorities
core_themes.claim: The ban will be enforced primarily by local authority Trading Standards, building on their existing role enforcing redress scheme membership and fee transparency requirements.

core_themes.name: Additional enforcement mechanisms under consideration
core_themes.claim: The Government is exploring further enforcement supports—such as a lead enforcement authority, increased data sharing, and wider regulation of the sector—to strengthen and make more consistent the enforcement of the ban.

core_themes.name: Tenant empowerment and education as enforcement tool
core_themes.claim: Educating and empowering tenants to challenge non-compliant agents, including routes to local authorities or the county court, is presented as key to effective enforcement and reducing the burden on local authorities.

core_themes.name: Penalty regime for non-compliance
core_themes.claim: The Government is considering whether breaches of the ban should attract civil penalties (potentially up to £30,000) or criminal sanctions such as banning orders, to provide an effective deterrent.

core_themes.name: Defining permitted charges and mitigating financial burden
core_themes.claim: Implementation will specify which charges remain permissible (such as holding deposits and tenant-caused service charges) and will explore ways to reduce the financial burden of deposits, such as capping or instalment models.
